title: Debugging a four-node FRDM-MCXA153 vehicle: an ESP32 I2C gateway that a bus scan kept breaking, and a silent PERC UART link traced to two wires in the wrong header holes

parts: You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude, assisting with an embedded firmware project.

  [diag] GW DOWN 0 ok / 2183 fail | PERC SILENT | ACT 147 ms | WEB silent

find the problems and the solution

Both failures are outside the MCX firmware, and your 2.3 V reading is the strongest clue you have. Here is what it says, what I changed, and what to measure next.

**The gateway: 2.3 V on both lines is a back-powered device, not a missing pull-up**

A floating bus drifts and reads near zero on a meter. A healthy bus reads 3.3 V. Both lines sitting steady at 2.3 V is 3.3 V minus a diode drop. That is what you get when a device on the bus has no supply, or its ground is not the MCX ground. Its input clamp diodes conduct the pull-up current into its dead rail, and since SDA and SCL land on the same rail they read the same voltage. Three candidates, in order of likelihood:

- ESP32 unpowered or browning out. Fed 9 V into VIN, a board with a SOT-23-5 regulator dies exactly this way.
- MPU6050 with SDA/SCL attached but VCC off. Its on-board 2.2 kOhm then pull the bus down into a dead rail.
- ESP32 ground not at the star point.

The measurements that settle it, black lead on MCX GND (J3-12): ESP32 3V3 pin must read 3.3 V, ESP32 GND pin must read 0.00 V, MPU6050 VCC must read 3.3 V. Then pull one node off the bus at a time. The bus jumps to 3.3 V when you unplug the culprit.

**PERC: the MCX side is provably the same as the working ACT side**

LPUART2's pins, mux, clock attach and interrupt handling match NXP's own example for this board exactly, and the sketch link code is identical to ACT's. So it is the wire, the divider, the ground, or the sketch flashed. The mikroBUS J5 pins 3 and 4 (RX/TX) are the same nets as PERC's link on J2-4/J2-2, so a wire one position off on J5 kills PERC and the gateway together.

**What I changed**

- link.c now records why the last gateway poll failed. The console prints it on the [diag] line and in the i2c scan: NAK, BUSY, TIMEOUT.
- Docs had the mikroBUS header backwards. NXP's example readmes put SDA on J5-6 and SCL on J5-5. FULL_SCHEMA.md, FIRMWARE.md, the three SVGs and the sketch headers now say J5.
- Firmware rebuilt clean, no warnings.

One caveat: led_blinky.c was being edited by another session while I worked, so I patched its current text rather than what I first read. Nothing is committed.

Two findings, and one of them reverses my previous advice.

**Status 903 means the wiring is fine**

903 is MAKE_STATUS(9,3), kStatus_LPI2C_FifoError. My switch statement did not cover it, which is why you got "unexpected". What matters is that the driver ranks the error flags in this order: pin-low timeout, arbitration lost, NAK, then FIFO error. A FIFO error is only ever reported when no NAK was seen.

There is more evidence in your paste. The line [GW] ESP32 NOT answering only prints on a change of state, and a change to "down" requires it to have been "up" first. The scan also reported the last gateway poll as "ok". Both say the gateway was working immediately before you ran i2c. Compared with 0 ok / 2183 fail this morning, the J5 rewiring worked.

**The scan is what broke it**

The probe read one byte from each address. Your ESP32 answers every request with exactly 49 bytes, so a one-byte read leaves 48 stranded in its slave transmit buffer, and every later poll is a frame behind for as long as that board stays powered. The diagnostic you reach for because the link is broken was breaking the link.

**Changes, all built clean**

- The probe is now an address-only zero-length write. Presence detection still works, and the gateway's buffer is never touched.
- The full status table, including 903, with a hint that says a FIFO error is not a wiring fault.
- The scan reports its own probe result instead of the background poll's status.
- LINK_GwResync() after anything that touches the bus, and an automatic controller re-init after six consecutive failures.
- A new gw command that dumps one raw 49-byte read with its status.

**What to do next**

Power-cycle the ESP32, since the stranded bytes survive a reset of the MCX but not of the ESP32. Flash the new binary, then run gw rather than i2c.

The gateway is fixed. The scan was the thing still lying, and my zero-length probe was the reason.

**What your two consoles prove**

The MCX shows 5072 ok / 24 fail, and the ESP32 shows reads climbing by 150 every 3 seconds. That is exactly the 50 Hz poll rate, with writes matching the 10 Hz telemetry, queue drained to zero and nothing dropped. Both ends agree the link is healthy. The J5 rewiring was the real fix.

**The scan was wrong, not the bus**

A zero-length write returns FIFO ERROR on LPI2C for every address, present or absent. I watched it report an empty bus while that same bus was serving five thousand successful reads. The command FIFO wants a data phase to go with the START, so an address-only transfer is not a valid probe on this controller. That was my change from the last round and it was a bad one.

The probe is now a one-byte write of a newline. It is harmless to both devices on this bus. The scan also now cross-checks the poll counters and says plainly that the bus works when the poll loop is succeeding.

**About those 24 failures**

They arrived as four runs of six, each ended by an automatic controller reset. Without that recovery the link would have stayed dead after the first one. If it starts costing you telemetry, the lever is LINK_GW_BAUDRATE, but I would leave it at 400 kHz while the failure rate stays under half a percent.

**PERC is the only remaining fault**

WEB silent is not a fault, the ESP32 shows ws 0, so the browser tab is simply not connected. Its own USB console splits the problem in one look: nothing at all means not flashed or not powered; [perc] lines with VCU SILENT means the forward path is broken; [perc] lines with VCU UP means the fault is the return path through the divider.

Try again

"VCU SILENT" plus the MCX saying "PERC SILENT" means both directions are dead while both boards are alive and running. That combination rules out a lot, and I ruled out more from here.

**The MCX side of that channel is sound**

I checked the built firmware rather than guessing. LPUART2_IRQHandler in the ELF resolves to our interrupt service routine, not the weak default handler, so the receive interrupt is really wired to the vector. The clock frequency helper treats instance 2 identically to instance 1. Since ACT runs the same code on LPUART1 and works, ground, baud rate and MCX firmware are all proven. The fault is off-chip or on the PERC board.

**Why the console couldn't tell you which**

PERC counted complete lines only. A line exists only if the byte stream was clean enough to contain a newline, so a disconnected wire and a stream of corrupted bytes both produced zero and printed the same word.

PERC now counts raw bytes separately and prints a verdict: rx 0 bytes / 0 lines means nothing arrives at all; rx N bytes / 0 lines means corruption, not a broken wire; N lines then silence means it worked once.

**One real fix, not just instrumentation**

Both echo pins were plain INPUT. With a sensor absent, unpowered, or missing its ground, those pins float and oscillate, firing the echo interrupt thousands of times a second. SoftwareSerial times its bits by counting CPU cycles, so a storm there breaks the link with every wire perfectly intact, and it would hit PERC and not ACT because only PERC attaches those interrupts.

They are now INPUT_PULLUP. With a sensor present this changes nothing. With a sensor absent the pin sits high and the range reports -1. A dead sensor should cost you that sensor, not the whole node.

This machine has no AVR toolchain, so unlike the MCX firmware this sketch is brace-balanced and hand-checked but not compiler-verified.

That output settles most of it.

**What your run proved**

Both sonars read real distances, 82 cm and 9 cm, so PERC's hardware and main loop are healthy. It sent 980 lines, so it transmits fine. The echo interrupt count is normal at roughly 33 per second, so the floating-pin theory is dead. And rx 0 bytes means not one byte has ever reached D4. That is not corruption, a baud mismatch or a level problem, because all of those still produce bytes.

The MCX side is now verified three independent ways. The interrupt handler resolves to our routine. The clock helper treats LPUART2 identically to LPUART1. And the ALT2 mux on both pins matches NXP's own generated example for this board. The fault is in the loom.

**The most likely fault**

D4 and D5 swapped, or the two wires in the wrong J2 holes. A swap produces exactly this signature: the MCX's transmit pin lands on PERC's D5, which is an output, so two drivers fight each other; the MCX's receive pin lands on PERC's D4, which is an input held high by an internal pull-up. Neither side ever sees data.

**A way to check without a meter**

New commands sense1 and sense2 on the MCX console. They take the receive pin off the LPUART and read it as a GPIO twice, once with the internal pull-down and once with the pull-up. Follows the pull means nothing is connected. High both times means driven at the idle level. Low both times means something is holding it down.

I also fixed something quietly wrong: framing, noise and parity errors were counted nowhere and cleared nowhere, so they latched. They are now counted per channel and shown on the diag line when non-zero.

Two separate things here, and the console one is good news.

**Your console is not frozen**

You are still seeing the diag line print. That line comes from diag_service(), which runs at the bottom of the same main loop that calls console_service(). If diag prints, the loop turns, so the firmware is alive and reading the console every pass. A frozen board is ruled out.

That makes it terminal-side. The MCX echoes every character it accepts, so no echo means no bytes are reaching it at all.

**frame err PERC 0 finishes the diagnosis**

Zero framing errors on PERC combined with zero bytes at PERC's end is conclusive. A wrong baud rate produces errors. A marginal level produces errors. A backwards divider produces errors. Silence with zero errors means there is no electrical activity on that pin at all.

So both directions are electrically dead while both boards are healthy and transmitting. It is not levels, not baud, not firmware. It is the two wires or the ground.

ACT's 12 framing errors are minor over a run that long and its link works.

**A freeze bug I fixed while looking**

The project bounds every I2C wait, with the reasoning written into the build file that a car must not be one loose wire away from a hang. The UART waits had exactly the same problem. UART_RETRY_TIMES defaults to zero, which the SDK header defines as waiting forever. Since LINK_SendLine reaches LPUART_WriteBlocking from the heartbeat, the drive repeat and the horn, a transmitter that stalled would have frozen the entire loop, console included.

It is now bounded to about 20 ms. Timeouts are counted and show as TX STALLED on the diag line. This was not the cause of what you just saw, but it would have bitten eventually.

Your screenshot shows a second, newer problem that I had not seen before, and it explains why nothing you do is helping.

**The gateway regressed, and the old recovery could never fix it**

You now have GW DOWN 0 ok / 80 fail BUSY (13 resets). Earlier today it was up with 5072 successful reads. BUSY means a bus line reads low before the transfer even starts, which is a slave holding the line down, not a controller problem. My automatic recovery was re-initialising the master, which is why you see thirteen identical resets and zero improvement.

I added the real cure. It takes both pins off the I2C peripheral, clocks the clock line by hand up to nine times until the slave lets go of the data line, generates a stop condition manually, then puts the pins back. It now runs automatically whenever a run of failures is BUSY. Since this appeared after you were rewiring for PERC, also check the ESP32 still has power and its ground.

**The console is not the firmware**

I checked three ways. The debug console initialises LPUART0 with receive enabled. The console reader polls the receive flag directly. And the LPUART0 interrupt vector is still the weak default handler, so no interrupt service routine is stealing bytes. Your diag line is still printing, which proves the main loop is turning.

So it is the host side. You are in the VS Code Serial Monitor with two monitors open, so make sure the send box you are typing into belongs to the COM3 one. Then check the line ending dropdown. If it is set to None, the board never sees a carriage return and never acts on the line. It needs CR or LF.

**You no longer need the console for the two tests that matter**

SW2 runs the PERC receive wire test. SW3 clocks the I2C bus free and then scans it. Both print their full result.

**PERC is unchanged and still conclusive**

[SW2] sense1 - is the PERC receive wire there?

   pulled down: LOW      pulled up: HIGH

   It followed the internal pull in both directions, and a pin
   with a driver on the far end cannot do that. The wire is

That is the answer. Nothing is connected to the MCX's receive pin for PERC.

Pulled down it read low, pulled up it read high, with zero transitions in a full second. A pin with a driver on the far end cannot do that. Meanwhile PERC is transmitting 320 lines and its sonars read 82 cm and 43 cm. Both boards are fine. The wire is simply not on that net, and since PERC also sees zero bytes on D4, the other wire is wrong too.

**Where they should actually go**

Skip the Arduino header. P3_14 and P3_15 appear on the mikroBUS socket as well, and the repo's own pin-conflict table confirms it: mikroBUS RX and TX are the same nets as Arduino D9 and D8. On the mikroBUS socket the pins are silkscreened by name, so there is nothing to count.

J5 pin 4, silkscreen TX, is P3_15 and goes to PERC D4 as a direct wire. J5 pin 3, silkscreen RX, is P3_14 and takes PERC D5 through the 1k/2k divider.

Keep the divider on the D5 side. P3_14 is not 5 V tolerant, only the two I2C pins are.

**Why you got it wrong on J2 but right on J5**

J1 through J4 are two-row footprints. "The second hole along" is pin 1 or pin 2 depending on which row your eye started in, and being one row out puts the wire on a completely different net that looks identical from above.

**Confirming the fix**

Watch PERC's [link] rx byte counter. The VCU sends a heartbeat once a second, so that number should start climbing within a second of the correct wire going in.

PERC is fixed. PERC 54 ms and PERC 42 ms mean ranges are arriving, and with ACT 124 ms alongside it, both Arduino links are up. Three of the four nodes are talking.

**A correction I owe you**

I told you earlier that a FIFO error proves the slave acknowledged, so it could not be a wiring fault. That was wrong, and your own output is what disproves it. The driver ranks NAK above FIFO error, but that ordering only decides between flags already latched when one status read sees them. On a multi-byte read the two are a race: the address goes into the command queue with the receive command behind it, an address NAK makes the master stop automatically, and the stale receive command then raises the FIFO flag. Whichever one the driver catches first is what it reports.

That is exactly why you see them alternating. NAK then FIFO ERROR on consecutive diag lines is not two faults. It is one fault reported two ways.

I fixed the hint text so it no longer sends you chasing the far end's timing.

**What your gateway line actually says**

The number that matters is 0 ok. Not one poll has succeeded since the board booted. That makes this a presence problem, not a protocol one, and the status word is nearly irrelevant. The firmware now leads with that instead of the status word whenever the success count is zero.

The gateway was running at 5072 successful polls earlier today, so something physical changed since. Most likely the I2C wires were disturbed while you were sorting out the PERC holes. Check that the ESP32 has power and is running esp32_gateway.ino, that SDA and SCL are still on the mikroBUS SDA and SCL pins, and that it still shares the MCX ground.
